To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the immunoassays for the measurement of indirect biomarkers of recombitant human GH, IGF-I, C-peptide, IGF-II and IGFBPs in urine samples, validated in house, can be used for doping control purposes.

Indirect biomarkers of rhGH and insulin misuse, evaluated by immunoassay, are affected by physical fitness and endurance training, with the only exception of urinary C-peptide that is higher in elite athletes than in recreational athletes and sedentiary individuals.

(1) indirect biomarkers of rhGH, IGF-I, insulin, IGF-II and IGFBP can be detected in the urine samples of athletes with different physical fitness and training levels, and (2) the variations observed among biomarkers of GH and insulin misuse should be considered in the setting of reference ranges for doping detection.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the validation of an immunoassay-based method for the indirect detection of recombinant hGH, IGF-I, C-peptide, IGF-II and IGFBP, and the evaluation of its application in the analysis of samples from athletes with different levels of fitness and endurance exercise.
the development of immunoassays for indirect biomarkers of GH and insulin misuse and their application to urine samples from subjects with different levels of endurance exercise and physical fitness.

the development and validation of immunoassays for indirect biomarkers of recombitant human GH (rhGH), IGF-I, IGFBP2, IGFBP3 and insulin (Cpeptide) and their application to the evaluation of their concentrations in urine samples of elite and recreational athletes and sedetnary individuals, with different levels of endurance exercise and physical fitness.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
immunoassay-based indirect biomarkers of GH and insulin misuse are not useful for doping control purposes in endurance athletes.
, in the present study, no evidence of GH or insulin use was found in the elite athletes.
immunoassay-based methods are not suitable for the detection of GH and insulin misuse in urine samples.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of the studied immunassays for the measurement of GH or insulin biomarkers in urine samples, as a tool to detect misuse, should be considered only as an additional tool to be used in combination with others.

the immunoassay-based measurements of indirect biomarkers of GH and insulin misuse are useful in detecting misuse of such substances in urine samples of athletes with different physical fitness and endurance training.
the studied biomarkers are not useful for the detection of GH or insulin abuse.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the immunoassays evaluated are suitable for the purpose of doping control and that the use of indirect biomarkers in urine samples is an interesting approach to be explored in the future.

the use of immunoassays for indirect biomarkers of GH, insulin-like growth factor and insulin misuse is feasible, although it is necessary to take into account the different characteristics of each biomarker.
the immunoassay-based indirect biomarkers of GH and insulin misuse can be measured in urine samples, but further studies are needed to validate the results and set up reference concentration ranges.
